newsitem.title: NORWAY: Norway central bank boss says hard to fight market.
newsitem.headline: Norway central bank boss says hard to fight market.

text.p: Norway's central bank governor Kjell Storvik said on Thursday it is still his goal to maintain a stable exchange rate for the runaway crown, but he conceded it is difficult to fight the market.

In an annual speech at Norges Bank, or central bank, Storvik said he hoped that some of the money now placed in the Norwegian currency by international investors would flow back into major European currencies once the economic situation abroad improved.

"I would like to underline that the operational guideline of a stable exchange rate stands firm," said Storvik. "However, it is not always an easy task to maintain a stable exchange rate in a world where market evaluations of the crown may have a major impact."
He has seen the crown appreciate by about three percent since the bank cut official interest rates on January 10 in a fruitless effort to stabilise the oil-backed currency at a weaker level.

"Although the central bank or others may argue and conclude that market perceptions are mistaken, it will not necessarily engender a correction in the market," he said. "Monetary policy must thus be conducted with considerable patience."
Two rate cuts in January were preceded by massive intervention by the bank, but none of the action had any depreciating effect on the crown.
Throwing in the towel, the bank said after its second rate cut in two days on January 10 that it would curb intervention temporarily and let the crown run its course for a while.
Storvik said that he now sensed "a perception in some quarters that the crown has appreciated on a permanent basis and will not return to its earlier range for a long time".

Statistics Norway said in an outlook earlier on Thursday it expected the import-weighted crown in 1997 and 1998 to stay five percent above its average level last year. A precondition was that the central bank kept interest rates unchanged, however.
Storvik did not say how he was going to fulfil the declared goal of bringing back the crown down to its former levels, but he said the bull run was understandable given the strong Norwegian economy.
Norway, which pumps over three million barrels of oil per day, is the world's second largest oil exporter after Saudi Arabia. It is also a major exporter of natural gas.
"The large current account and government budget surpluses, combined with favourable developments in output and employment, are factors which traditionally point to rising prosperity," Storvik said.
"Market participants naturally tend to assume that such a rise in prosperity will translate into a stronger currency."

Storvik said the huge capital flows into Norway may partly be ascribed to the sluggishness of the major economies in continental Europe and the uncertainty around future exchange rate movements under European Monetary Union (EMU).

"If this is the case, it is also possible that some of this capital will flow back into the major European currencies when the economic situation on the continent is normalised and the uncertainty surrounding EMU subsides, with the effects this may have on the crown's exchange rate," he said.

The crown on Thursday evening stood at about 95.85 on the inverse ECU index of European currencies, a theoretical basket used by the bank to monitor the strength of the currency. Against the mark, the crown held its ground at 3.92 crowns.
